book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West

chapters.file: ch22 - Wait, Did I Hit Pause Where’d the Remote Get to . ..md
chapters.relation: Seng takes up the fan phenomenon of syncing The Wizard of Oz with Pink Floyd's Dark Side of the Moon and tests the three explanations fans offer: authorial intent (rejected on Pink Floyd's own repeated denials), Jungian synchronicity (rejected as needlessly complex, with the L. Frank Baum coat worn by Frank Morgan as the test case), and pure fluke. He argues the symmetries (the cash-register intro of 'Money' as Dorothy enters Technicolor, 'The Great Gig in the Sky' over the cyclone) are neither objective nor mind-created reality, but meanings made by a third factor in the experience: the viewer whose perceptual habits, in Dewey's and Louise Rosenblatt's sense, supply interpretations like reading the color-splash as prosperity or as the cost of Dorothy's lost innocence. Dorothy's own longing for home becomes the emblem of how habit, not reasoning, governs what we perceive and like.

Auxier asks why the flying monkeys and the shriveling feet of the Wicked Witch of the East give children lifelong nightmares, and answers with a phenomenology of three frightening sequences in escalating duration: the instant shriveling shot, the five-minute cyclone (paired with 'The Great Gig in the Sky' in the Dark Side of the Rainbow sync), and the monkey air-raid. Kierkegaard's Concept of Anxiety supplies the depth psychology: innocence is ignorance, and the child's dreaming spirit projects its own nothing outward, fastening fear onto figures like the monkeys (who are, he notes, played by the Munchkin actors themselves). Merleau-Ponty's lived body versus habit body explains the mechanics: cinema seizes the body's usual 'tour of inspection,' Fleming manipulates active and passive synthesis (the scoreless build-up to the window blow, the barely noticed arsenal of weapons in the Haunted Forest, the dimming lights), and children construct a rigid, inescapable habit body within a single viewing, so the nightmare is the monkey inside our own projected world.

chapters.file: ch24 - V - No Place Like Home.md

chapters.relation: Flamm and Rea read the Oz story as an existential fable of the appearance-reality distinction in human development: children delight in admitted unrealities while adults live by ideals, and Dorothy's growth is learning to trade the one for the other, dramatized in the China Princess scene where Dorothy must abandon her plan to keep the animated figure frozen on Aunt Em's mantel. The Wizard embodies the American humbug in the P.T. Barnum mold, forcing green spectacles on the Emerald City's citizens so the city only appears green, science as technical illusion without deeper ideals, while the silver shoes reveal that the imaginative escape Dorothy sought was hers all along. Her homecoming is therefore bittersweet and existential: she can never return to the Kansas she left, 'but she can return to herself,' carrying the crayon box of self-chosen ideals with which to color her own reality.

Seng maps Dorothy's journey onto Plato's cave allegory: Kansas is the cave of shadows, Oz the painful ascent into light, and the crucial shared point is Socrates' demand that the freed prisoner go back down into the cave, which explains why Dorothy, once enlightened, must return to gray Kansas bearing self-knowledge. He surveys the film adaptations (1910, Semon's 1925, Eshbaugh's 1933, Fleming's 1939, Return to Oz, and The Wiz) to show that each rewrites 'home' as self-knowledge rather than a place, culminating in Glinda's The Wiz speech, 'If we know ourselves, we're always home, anywhere.' Kierkegaard's contrast between recollection and repetition then sorts the homecomings: Baum's Dorothy wills recollection of what was lost, while Diana Ross's Dorothy wills repetition, holding to her self amid change, which Seng says Kierkegaard regards as the equivalent of faith.

Bickham asks why Dorothy is so eager to leave heroic, Technicolor Oz for the gray, childless, Gulch-dominated farm, and whether, like Hamlet's delay, her rash choice can be evaluated as hers rather than her author's. Aristotle's account of the good life as the exercise of our highest capacities, requiring friends and material goods, makes Oz look like the better home for the competent twelve- or thirteen-year-old he takes Dorothy to be, against the hedonisms of Aristippus, Epicurus, and Bentham and Plato's body-denying dualism. But caring about Dorothy first needs defending from the paradox of fiction, which he works through Currie's simulation theory and Walton's make-believe emotions before dissolving the puzzle: storytelling suspends the reign of logic, so wishing Dorothy well is natural. Finally Heidegger's being-toward-death shows 'happily ever after' is impossible anywhere, and he throws the problem to the reader: write a happy ending for Dorothy in Kansas.

chapters.file: ch28 - You Can Go Home Again.md
chapters.relation: Fortune stages the movie as a morality play between two conceptions of personhood: the Wizard is an atomist, a self-sufficient ball from the Chuck E. Cheese ball pit who is the same humbug in Omaha or Oz and who reduces heart, brains, and courage to a testimonial, a diploma, and a medal, while Dorothy is a relationalist, a pineapple chunk that belongs on one particular pizza, a person constituted by her web of relations to home. 'There's no place like home' is therefore the relationalist's slogan, an acceptance of home for everything it is, good and bad, with Toto's fate still unresolved under Miss Gulch's law. He closes by suggesting the film's delayed television-era triumph is existential nostalgia: modern, rootless, ear-budded Americans keep watching because the relationalist country it mourns is 'what's in our blood.'

chapters.file: ch29 - VI - Something Wicked This Way Comes.md

chapters.relation: Sailors convicts Dorothy of being the stereotypical female of Baum's and Fleming's versions, disowning responsibility for killing both witches and living to please others, then contrasts her with Elphaba of Wicked as a feminist hero who leaves home, protects Animals, and mixes 'hot' male and 'cold' female anger into a single fury. She reads Elphaba's indeterminate gender through Marilyn Frye's point that easily identifiable groups are the easiest to oppress, through de Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but becomes a woman' and Mill's line that the 'nature of women' is an eminently artificial thing. Singer's liberation logic, together with the Wollstonecraft-Taylor 'Vindication of the Rights of Brutes' episode and the ecofeminist link between the oppression of women and animals, is applied to Elphaba's Animal-rights activism and her position as 'neither man nor beast,' before the Witch's mirror recognition of Dorothy forces the author to soften her verdict.

chapters.file: ch31 - As Nasty as I Wanna Be.md
chapters.relation: Greene asks whether Maguire's Elphaba is really wicked, first clearing away her reputation (she adopts the 'Wicked Witch' name because 'it liberates you from convention,' echoing Glaucon's challenge in the Republic about the just person with an unjust reputation and vice versa) and then her nature (the midwife-biting birth, green skin, and witchcraft establish no vampire-like evil essence, since Glinda and Nor are good witches). Following Hume's view that morality is not found in the world but in our assessments, he treats wickedness as a matter of performing actions we judge evil, and weighs Elphaba's life under both headings: good intentions with horrific outcomes (the bees that kill the chef, the icicle that kills Manek, Sarima's family executions) and bad intentions with none (her two failed attempts on Madame Morrible). The verdict is deliberately suspended: if she is wicked at all, it can only be through the consequences of her actions.

Durand begins from Hume's moral sentiments, the way first impressions (Miss Gulch, the farmer-actors, Professor Marvel) fix our judgments, and shows how Wicked delivers the new information that muddies them, relocating villainy from the green Witch to the green Wizard: an alien despot who scorns Oz's communal moral sense ('I am beyond that lisping childish recital of wrongs and rights'), stations an army of observation at the Witch's borders, and schemes to annex Munchkinland after Nessarose's fall. Marx's 'opium of the masses' frames the religion of Frex and Nessarose as the tool that first pacified, then repressed, the Munchkinlanders, while the Wizard's 'reunification' that is really annexation shows imperial ideology at work. Elphaba's own 'wickedness' comes out as habituated vengeance and an embraced reputation, so the title question is whether she is inept rather than evil, 'a bad witch, but not a wicked one,' and no worse than the Wizard who is merely 'a very bad wizard.'

chapters.file: ch33 - Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf.md
chapters.relation: Auxier tells the history of matriarchy theory from Bachofen onward, whose stages (Tellurian earth-motherhood, lunar water cults, then Dionysian and Apollonian fire clearing the way for patriarchy) were adapted by Nietzsche in The Birth of Tragedy, quoted by Engels, and developed by Jane Ellen Harrison, Jung, and Gimbutas. He then reads Maguire's Oz myths as survivals of that declining matriarchy: the Kumbric Witch as the Tellurian earth stage, Mother Yackle's Philosophy Club as degraded Dionysian rites, the silver slippers as the totality of feminine power, and the Silver-slippers portrait Boq finds as the earth-to-water transition, noting that Plato's victory of reason over myth is what dragged women's traditional authority down with it. The chapter's payoff is its title claim: Elphaba is Virginia Woolf, her Charmed Circle the Bloomsbury Group, her terror of water and fiery, watery death a repetition of Woolf's drowning 'baptism' under patriarchy.

chapters.file: ch36 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy.md

holes.name: Appearance and Reality
holes.what: The classic distinction between how things seem to us and how they really are, and the question of whether appearances can be trusted to disclose reality.
holes.why: Chapter 25's entire reading of the green spectacles, the humbug Wizard, and Dorothy's maturation is organized around the appearance-reality distinction, and the taxonomy has no slug for it.

holes.name: Repetition and Recollection
holes.what: Kierkegaard's pair from Repetition: recollection looks backward longingly at what is lost, while genuine repetition 'recollects forward,' re-appropriating life faithfully with a stable self amid change.
holes.why: Chapter 26 uses exactly this pair to distinguish the various Dorothys' homecomings, recollecting old Kansas versus willing repetition with self-knowledge as in The Wiz, and no taxonomy slug covers it.

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle that we appear to have genuine emotions for characters we know do not exist, though caring about non-existent people seems impossible; theories include Currie's simulation and Walton's make-believe emotions.
holes.why: Chapter 27 must dissolve this paradox to justify asking whether Dorothy should have stayed in Oz, since wishing the best for a fictional girl has to make sense first.

holes.name: Matriarchy Theory (Bachofen's Mutterrecht)
holes.what: Bachofen's theory that human culture originated in mother-right and evolved through Tellurian, lunar, Dionysian and Apollonian stages before patriarchy, carried forward by Harrison, Engels, Jung, and Gimbutas.
holes.why: Chapter 33 is built on this tradition, reading the Kumbric Witch, the Lurline cult, Mother Yackle, and the silver slippers as survivals of a declining matriarchy, and the chapter insists it is not feminist philosophy proper.

holes.name: The Axial Age
holes.what: The era of 'paradigmatic individuals' (Confucius, Laozi, Socrates, Buddha, Jesus) whose reforms moved religion from visible sun-cults toward universal, invisible ethical order.
holes.why: Chapter 33 presents Maguire's Oz as a thought experiment in history with no Axial Age, which lets matriarchal folk religion survive two extra millennia alongside an ineffectual Unionist monotheism.
